one_liner: Ahead-of-time compiler from a NumPy-flavoured Python subset to C++17 extension modules; 11x-2096x faster than CPython on loop kernels.
what_it_does: Pythran translates a Python module, annotated with '# pythran export f(int, float[:,:])' comment lines (or a side .pythran file), into heavily templated C++ that is compiled into a native extension module with the same name and interface. The original .py file stays valid Python, so the same source runs uncompiled under CPython. It supports functions, lambdas, comprehensions, list/dict/set, exceptions and a partial NumPy API, but not classes, heterogeneous containers (other than tuples) or big integers.
how_it_is_fast: Type inference from the export signatures lets it instantiate monomorphic, heavily templated C++ (the MANUAL's description), so element-wise loops over NumPy arrays become plain C++ loops with no interpreter dispatch or boxing, which the C++ compiler can auto-vectorise. NumPy expressions are handled in that template layer with laziness analysis and expression combiners (named in recent commits and the 0.19.0 Changelog) to avoid intermediate arrays, with optional explicit SIMD through xsimd (-DUSE_XSIMD) and OpenMP from '#omp parallel for' comment annotations (-fopenmp). Range and alias analysis (helped by asserts) speeds indexing, and the GIL is released while the compiled function runs.
when_to_use: Hot numeric kernels written as explicit Python loops that index NumPy arrays element by element (stencils, finite differences, graph shortest paths): 130x-2096x over CPython 3.12 in the pyccel-benchmarks run.
You want to keep one pure-Python source file that still runs uncompiled, with types given only in '# pythran export' comments rather than Cython-style declarations.
Code that mixes NumPy array expressions with loops and can use the optional xsimd vectorisation and '#omp parallel for' OpenMP loops (neither was enabled in the cited benchmark).
Building wheels with setuptools or Meson for Linux, macOS or Windows (clang-cl) where a C++17 compiler is available at build time.
Recursive integer code such as Ackermann (169x over CPython) as long as values fit in a C long.
when_not_to_use: Code that already spends its time inside vectorised NumPy calls: the one baseline that used NumPy slicing (FD Laplace) gained only 10.9x, and open issues report Pythran slower than NumPy on array assignment (#2095), some broadcasting patterns above ~20 columns (#2019) and slower than SciPy on long-double convolution (#2275).
Object-oriented code: classes are not supported (the Splines benchmark, a class, does not compile), nor are heterogeneous lists or arbitrary-precision integers.

Small-array ODE-style kernels that pass function arguments and operate on 1-element arrays: Pythran trailed Pyccel 3.8x on Euler, 4.1x on Midpoint Explicit and 5.6x-37x on Midpoint Fixed in the same table.
Environments without a C++17 compiler at install/build time, or where 2-7.5 CPU s of compile time per module (higher than Pyccel's 1.6-3.1 s in the same run) matters.
Calls on small inputs where argument conversion dominates: non-ndarray arguments are deep-copied at the Python boundary (open issue #2012).

integration.dependencies: Python >=3.7, ply, gast ~0.7.0, beniget ~0.5.0, numpy, setuptools; Boost and xsimd headers (vendored in the PyPI package, may be unvendored by conda-forge and distros); a BLAS (configurable: none, scipy-openblas, openblas, mkl and others); a C++17 compiler at build time
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 compiler from 0.19.0 (Changelog 'Bump C++ dependency to C++17'); the MANUAL FAQ still lists g++ 4.9+ and clang++ 3.5+, which is stale; Python 3.7+
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS (PyPI classifiers); Windows described as ongoing, with Visual Studio 2017 or clang-cl; 32-bit compatibility improved in 0.19.0; xsimd SIMD optional
integration.thread_safety: Releases the GIL during the compiled call; internal reference counting is non-atomic for non-OpenMP code unless built with -DTHREAD_SAFE_REF_COUNT (small penalty); free-threading support added in 0.18.0 via a config option
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the compiled module is a drop-in import replacement for the .py module, but only for code inside Pythran's subset (no classes, homogeneous containers, C long integers) with export signatures added

gotchas: Harness flaw in the cited benchmark: pyccel-benchmarks' run_benchmarks.py never compares outputs between CPython and the compiled versions, so with -ffast-math a numerically different result would go unnoticed; FD Laplace also stops on a relative-tolerance test, so its iteration count (and time) can differ between implementations.

The cited table is not a scalar-loop-only baseline as the record says: FD Laplace's CPython code uses NumPy slice expressions (hence only 10.9x), and the ODE kernels (Euler, Midpoint, RK4) run on 1-element arrays with a function argument.

The benchmark's pythran_gnu.config defines no USE_XSIMD and no -fopenmp, so the measured numbers use g++ auto-vectorisation only; it also passes -std=c++14, which matched 0.18.1 but conflicts with 0.19.0's C++17 requirement, so copy it with care.
Integers are C long (system-dependent width, no overflow promotion), and non-ndarray arguments are deep copies, so in-place mutation of a list argument is not visible to the caller.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Pythran over Pyccel when the kernel uses richer Python (comprehensions, dicts, sets, exceptions, polymorphic helpers) or NumPy expressions, and over Cython when you want the source to stay plain Python with types only in export comments. In the same run Pythran had the fastest M-D (36.3 ms) and Dijkstra (pythran_intel 16.8 ms) rows while Pyccel won Ackermann, Euler, Midpoint and RK4. Shed Skin or Codon fit whole programs with classes better, since Pythran does not support classes.
verified_claims_summary: In the Pyccel developers' pyccel-benchmarks GitHub Actions run (ubuntu-latest shared VM, CPU model and g++ version unrecorded, 2026-08-03), Pythran 0.18.1 built with g++ -O3 -march=native -mavx -ffast-math ran 12 numeric kernels 10.9x (FD Laplace) to 2096x (FD Poisson) faster than CPython 3.12, geometric mean about 264x (derived from page data), timed with python3 -m timeit best of 5, compile time excluded; Splines did not compile.
status_note: Actively maintained (0.19.0 on PyPI 2026-08-17, commits through 2026-09-14), BSD-3-Clause and packaged on PyPI, conda-forge, Arch and Fedora, but 140 open issues include a long tail of performance gaps versus NumPy, SciPy and Julia.
